title: The Idea of Public Reason Revisited
argument: Rawls asks how political justification should proceed when free and equal citizens hold reasonable but conflicting comprehensive doctrines. His answer is that public reason requires reciprocal justification: citizens owe one another political reasons they can reasonably expect others to accept. Political conceptions of justice must be freestanding and address the basic structure. Political autonomy need not prescribe autonomous living throughout private life. Public reason does not ban religious or comprehensive reasons. Under the proviso, such reasons may enter political discussion provided appropriate political reasons are supplied in due course. Reciprocal political reasons can therefore govern common justification while leaving room for comprehensive reasons and private ethical diversity.
review: The main surviving concern is comparative. Why should justification rest on shared political reasons rather than on sincere convergence from person-relative reasons? Completeness and voluntariness are largely acknowledged limits of application.
use: criteria for reciprocal justification, especially for testing the Heath project, though not an automatic verdict on every institution.

title: Carnap, the Ramsey-Sentence and Realistic Empiricism
argument: Psillos asks whether Carnap's division of a theory into its Ramsey sentence and its Carnap sentence secures a neutral reconciliation of realism and empiricism. He reconstructs the separation of a theory's existential Ramsey content from an analytic Carnap conditional and argues that it does not. Newman-style realizability arguments threaten unrestricted structural content. The natural response is to restrict admissible realizers to natural properties, but this appears to add the very commitments a purely structural account was meant to avoid. Psillos concludes that formal structural reconstruction does not by itself settle the semantic commitments at stake between realists and empiricists.
review: The Newman challenge survives, but the step from structural triviality to the defeat of Carnapian neutrality remains contestable, as does the handling of admissibility restrictions. The result does not refute every Ramsey method or structural realism.
use: auditing which additional semantic commitments a structural reconstruction requires.

title: Patches, Patchworks, and Epsilon Terms: A Neo-Carnapian Account of Theoretical Terms in Science
authors: Matteo De Benedetto, Elio La Rosa
cite: Journal of Philosophical Logic 53: 1495–1517 (2024); online 14 September 2024
argument: De Benedetto and La Rosa ask how Carnap's epsilon-term account of theoretical terms can handle scientific patchworks, where the same theoretical vocabulary receives different local interpretations. They argue that naively globalizing local roles by conjunction fails. Their construction instead quantifies each patch separately and retains cross-patch identities and differences as glue. It then introduces epsilon definitions intended to preserve the analytic/synthetic division. The paper presents a flat-case theorem and a rephrasing of the construction. The result is offered as a contextual neo-Carnapian account of theoretical terms, meant to extend Carnap's analytic/synthetic distinction to patchwork science.
review: Our review found a coordinate-choice problem in the printed construction: separately chosen coordinates can come from different patches, satisfying no patch. A shared-context choice plausibly repairs it. This is a reviewer finding, not an erratum, author admission, or universal refutation.
use: optional advanced formal study, not machinery to import without repair.

title: On the logic of what matters
cite: The Philosophical Quarterly, advance article pqag067; published 23 September 2026
argument: Muñoz asks whether cyclic evaluative intuitions can be accommodated without giving up the transitivity of betterness. He proposes keeping betterness transitive while distinguishing a further relation, defeat, that need not be transitive. On this view, the cyclic intuitions may concern defeat rather than betterness. The proposal is motivated by an analogy with Parfit's separation of personal identity from what matters in survival. Drawing on Yablo's idea of logical subtraction, Muñoz suggests that subtracting transitivity could leave a relation that retains important evaluative content. He concludes, as a conceptual proposal, that distinguishing defeat from betterness may preserve both transitive betterness and the significance of cyclic intuitions.
review: The surviving concern is whether removing a three-variable transitivity condition leaves an independently meaningful evaluative relation. This is a substantive gap rather than a demonstrated fatal flaw.
use: separating logical order from what matters, though the paper does not supply a complete replacement decision theory.

title: The Possibility of Parity
argument: Chang asks whether comparable alternatives must be better, worse, or equally good, or whether there can be a further comparative relation. She argues for the possibility of parity: two items can be comparable without one being better than the other and without their being equally good. Small-improvement and chaining arguments are used to show comparability outside the familiar trichotomy. She then argues that such cases are not merely instances of vagueness. Her conclusion is that better, worse, and equally good need not exhaust comparability. Parity is a possible additional relation, distinct from both incomparability and indeterminacy.
review: Chaining needs a substantive premise that comparability is preserved along the chain. The argument against vagueness is less decisive than the broader challenge to the trichotomy. No fatal flaw is established.
use: distinguishing parity, equality, incomparability and indeterminacy, with a productive contrast with Muñoz.

title: Categories of Art
argument: Walton asks how the category in which an artwork is perceived affects the aesthetic properties it appears to have, and what makes a category correct. He argues that apparent aesthetic properties depend on the perceived category. Features that are standard, variable, or contra-standard relative to that category explain the shifts. His Guernica example shows how the same perceptible features yield different aesthetic appearances under different categories. Correct categories are constrained partly by artistic history and intention. They are not fixed merely by surface properties or by whichever classification makes the work most appealing. Such historical facts help determine correct appreciation without replacing category-sensitive perception.
review: The narrower surviving concern is that the case for historically privileged correctness is incomplete, while the account of category-sensitive perception survives. The correctness criteria are defeasible, and correct appreciation implies no obligation to appreciate that way.
use: foundational machinery for analytic aesthetics, not an algorithm for classification.
